newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says EU Parliament plans office, Europe say.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says EU Parliament plans office, Europe say.

text.p: Taiwan said on Thursday that the European Parliament had committed to opening a liaison office in Taipei, a move sure to incense the Nationalist-ruled island's arch rival communist China.
European Parliament officials denied the move, but said the parliament had asked the European Union's executive Commission to set up an information office in Taipei.
"The European Parliament doesn't open liaison offices anywhere in the world. It must be a misunderstanding," an official with the EU assembly's foreign affairs committee told Reuters.

Taiwan's Foreign Minister John Chang, back from a secrecy-cloaked visit to Europe and west Africa, said members of the European Parliament had approved several resolutions on the future of Europe's ties with China and Taiwan, and one of them was to set up an office in Taipei, Beijing's rival since 1949.
"The European Parliament decided ... after my speech that they were going to set up a liaison office in Taipei," Chang said on his return from Europe and Africa.
"The parliament has approved a budget to establish such an office... No date had been set."

Chang said he kept his Brussels visit secret because during a previous visit to Belgium in 1996, the European Parliament had invited him to deliver a speech on the condition that there would be no media coverage.
"We had to make sure that our efforts to increase our substantive ties with Europe would not be thwarted by the pressure of the Chinese communists," he said.

China, which has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split the two in 1949, has exerted a diplomatic squeeze on the island by warning other countries against forging ties with Taipei.
Chang indicated there were no significant diplomatic breakthroughs during his 11-day trip that included stays in Belgium, Luxembourg, Guinea Bissau and Senegal.

He said South Africa, which told Taiwan in November that it would switch diplomatic ties in 1997 to Beijing, had agreed to a third round of talks in Taipei in June to negotiate the nature of bilateral ties after the change.
"Only when we reach agreement would the suspended economic cooperation programmes and direct flights be resumed," Chang added.
Taiwan suspended economic aid and flight links with South Africa in December after failing to convince Pretoria to drop its plan to switch diplomatic recognition to Beijing.

He reiterated that Taiwan's relations with most of its other allies were firm, especially with Panama which local news media had speculated might switch ties to Beijing to maintain its shipping and other interests in Hong Kong.

China, which will retake Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, has said that Taiwan's allies would not be allowed to maintain their consulates in Hong Kong after the British colony is handed back to the mainland.
Nine of Taiwan's 30 diplomatic allies, mostly impoverished states in Central America and Africa, maintain consulates in Hong Kong.
